abstract: The Cdc14 phosphatase plays essential roles in meiotic chromosome metabolism and cell-cycle progression, yet the cellular pathways capable of compensating for reduced Cdc14 function remain poorly understood. To explore these connections, we performed a multicopy suppressor screen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using a mutant CDC14 allele that severely impairs sporulation. UV-excited ascospore-wall autofluorescence enabled the rapid screening of approximately 14,400 transformants, while subsequent microscopy provided quantitative validation of sporulation phenotypes. Photographic image processing facilitated candidate recovery, and a complementary computational analysis of archived images established the reproducibility of fluorescence-associated detections across different acquisition conditions. Genetic screening and independent plasmid retransformation identified four genomic-library plasmids that reproducibly enhanced sporulation. Molecular characterisation of the strongest suppressors revealed genomic regions associated with chromatin regulation and nuclear-pore organisation. Further analysis prioritised two particularly promising candidate genes: RCO1, encoding a component of the Rpd3S histone-deacetylase complex, and POM34, encoding an integral membrane nucleoporin. Suppressor activity was retained in a reduced POM34-containing construct, strengthening its candidacy for further functional investigation. Together, these findings establish an effective fluorescence-guided strategy for multicopy suppressor discovery and reveal promising genetic connections between Cdc14-dependent meiotic progression, chromatin regulation and nuclear architecture.
